Alice Huang ran Megaspeed, a Singapore company that bought Nvidia servers and kept them in Malaysia, where Chinese companies rented them over the internet. American intelligence was listening to her the whole time, and in her calls it found Jensen's name. For almost two years, nobody told him.

Who should have warned him?

text: In Singapore, the boss of the most valuable company on earth is having dinner with a Chinese spy. He's Jensen Huang, who runs Nvidia. She's Alice Huang, no relation, and she runs one of his biggest customers. But here's the strange part. Somewhere nearby, American agents are taking pictures. They know exactly who she is. Jensen has no idea. >> To our customers. >> To friends. >> Under that table, her company is buying billions of dollars of his chips, the kind China isn't allowed to have. This is the story of how China got a spy into that seat and who was watching. It starts with a phone call from Washington. But to see why that call mattered, you need to know who picked it up because the man in the leather jacket didn't start at the top. He started in a bathroom in Kentucky. Jensen's story begins in Taiwan. At nine, he and his older brother were put on a plane to relatives in America. To pay for a good school, his parents sold almost everything they owned. >> Oneida Baptist Institute, a boarding school in Kentucky. >> Very strict. >> Strict is good. >> It wasn't a fancy boarding school. It was a reform school for troubled kids, and the relatives had signed them up by mistake. His brother was sent to work the school's tobacco fields. Jensen got the bathrooms, a hundred teenage boys worth every single day. >> I just wish they would be a bit more careful. >> His roommate was 17, covered in tattoos and knife scars and taped up from his latest fight. He was the toughest kid in the school, and he couldn't read. >> What's this say? >> I can teach you. >> Then I teach you the bench press. >> Deal. Decades later, Jensen gave that school $2 million for a new building. It's called Huang Hall. The boy who cleaned its bathrooms put his name on the front door. At 15, he took the graveyard shift at Denny's. >> Dishes first, and then? >> Then bus boy. Then, if lucky, waiter. >> >> And then? >> >> Then, more dishes. >> And in 1993, he went back to Denny's, not to work, to start a company. In a corner booth in East San Jose, Jensen and two engineer friends, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, sketched a chip for 3D graphics. He liked the place because it was quieter than home, and the coffee was cheap. >> Anything else, boys? >> A graphics chip. >> We have pancakes. >> Then three more coffees. >> Each founder put in $200, $600, about the price of a used couch to take on the biggest chip companies in the world. It nearly died. When its make-or-break chip finally shipped in 1997, Nvidia had about one month of payroll left. The company's unofficial motto became >> Our company is 30 days from going out of business. >> So, how long have we got? >> 30 days. >> And if the new chip doesn't sell? >> 29. >> It sold about a million of them in four months. And here's the trick that later made it a giant. A normal computer chip is one brilliant chef cooking a whole wedding dinner, one plate at a time. Nvidia's chip is 10,000 line cooks, each flipping one pancake at the very same moment. For video games, that meant explosions. Then researchers noticed that artificial intelligence needs exactly that, millions of tiny sums all at once. Chat GPT was trained on a supercomputer built from tens of thousands of Nvidia chips. And suddenly, every AI company on Earth was standing in the same line. >> One of everything, please. >> Take a number. >> 40,000? >> >> That's your place in line. >> By 2025, about 86 of every $100 spent on AI chips went to Nvidia. In 2023, Denny's put a plaque on the booth. It calls it the booth that launched a $1 trillion company. At the party, the boss of that company put on an apron, balanced 10 plates up his arm, and served the tables. >> Still remember how? >> Dishes first. >> Two years later, Nvidia became the first company ever worth $5 trillion. Every dollar the three of them put into that booth had become about $8 billion. The kid who scrubbed the toilets in Kentucky now holds the key to artificial intelligence. And when he talks about who should be allowed to buy his chips, Washington listens. >> Every AI lab on earth needs this man. >> Then so do we. >> That made him the one man China needed most. October 2022, Washington calls Nvidia. >> Your best AI chips can't be sold to China anymore. >> And the slower ones we made just for China? >> Those too. >> China, $17 billion a year, 13% of everything we sell. >> Was. How many chips do we need for a real AI? >> Tens of thousands. >> And one costs? >> About $30,000, a new car per chip. >> And how many can we buy? >> Zero. >> By Jensen's own account, Nvidia's share of China's market went from 95% to zero. And he told Washington so every chance he got. >> They're nanoseconds behind us. We've got to go compete. >> So China couldn't buy the chips, but it could get close to the man who makes them and who argues with Washington about who gets to buy them. That's a job for China's Ministry of State Security, the MSS. Picture the FBI and the CIA in one building. It doesn't crack the safe. It befriends the man with the key. Nobody outside Beijing has said when Alice Huang was recruited, but an American memo later wrote down her job. >> This man makes the chips and Washington listens to him. >> So what do I steal? >> Nothing. You learn what he knows. You help him see things our way. >> Why would he even talk to me? >> Because you'll be his customer. >> And then? >> We make friends. >> The key belonged to one man, and that man likes everybody. In 2023, a Chinese and cloud company called Seven Road split off its business outside China, moved it to Singapore and renamed it Mega Speed. The managing director was Alice Huang. >> We make phone games. >> Now we make super computers. >> Since when? >> Since Singapore. >> Address? >> Singapore. America trusts Singapore. >> Business? >> Cloud computing. A cloud company needs mountains of chips and nobody asks why. >> And the chips go where? >> Data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia. Not one chip goes to China. >> Then how does China use them? >> It rents them. >> Imagine a country that isn't allowed to buy cars. So you buy the cars, park them just over the border, and rent out the keys by the hour. Chinese companies, Alibaba among them, rented time on the chips the same way, and the chips never entered China. >> Can we buy your chips? >> No, but you can rent them. >> By the hour? >> By the warehouse. >> At the end of 2023, everything Mega Speed owned came to about $33 million. A nice little company, and not one the boss of Nvidia had any reason to meet. So she went and found him. Jensen Huang isn't hard to meet. The former Denny's dishwasher now runs a company worth about $4.5 and he still treats every customer like a regular. As his spokesman later put it, >> Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year. >> She was about to become one of those thousands. June 2024 in Taipei, the big chip show Computex has just ended, and Jensen goes for whiskey with people from the AI world. Someone takes photos. In them, right beside him, is Alice Huang. >> >> Who haven't I met? >> Alice, Mega Speed, Singapore. >> Singapore? What are you building? >> A cloud company. Something big. >> Then welcome to the table. >> Nobody looks at those photos twice. Later, someone will. That month, at MegaSpeed's Malaysian arm, the paperwork starts. >> What do we put up as collateral? Everything. The whole Malaysian business? The whole business, every last desk. And the lender is? >> Owned by Alibaba. >> And the buying began. >> A Singapore company wants servers. How many? Yes. Shipment 100. Shipment 150. Shipment 200. >> What's in them? >> Nvidia's best. Nearly $2 billion worth. >> At $30,000 a chip? That's about 60,000 chips. >> A parking lot of 60,000 new cars in 1 year. >> End of 2023, we had $33 million. >> Yes. >> End of 2024, we have $3 billion. >> Yes. >> 2.9 billion of it is deposits. >> From who? >> Refundable. >> From Refundable. >> About 90 times bigger in 1 year. If a lemonade stand went from $33 to 3,000 in a year, its parents would have questions. Then, late in 2024, an official from America's Commerce Department walks into one of the Malaysian data centers. It's supposed to be full of humming AI servers. >> Where's the data center? >> You're standing in it. >> These are boxes. >> Very advanced boxes. >> I'm opening an investigation. >> The inspector wrote it all down, and nothing happened because on paper, nothing looked wrong. Every sale went to Singapore or Malaysia, not China. When Nvidia sent people to check her sites, every chip was exactly where it should be. Jensen later said they had counted every one. That was the whole trick. The chips stayed put, and China rented them over the internet. What almost nobody knew was that American spies were already listening to her. When American spy agencies listen to a foreign target and that target talks to an American, the reports hide the American's name. They just say an American citizen. >> She's talking to an American citizen. >> Then request the name. >> It's Jensen Huang. >> Does he know who she is? >> Our read? No. >> How far back does it go? >> June 2024, a whiskey bar in Taipei. >> Then we watch. >> So where did all those servers come from? Mostly from Avras, the American arm of Inspur, a Chinese server giant partly owned by the Chinese state and on America's blacklist. >> Inspur? You're on the list. >> I'm Avras, the American son. >> Avras, not on here. >> Thanks. >> December 2024 to January 2026, $4.6 billion of equipment in. >> And from Avras? >> $4 billion. >> Malaysia was the older cousin who buys beer for kids who are too young, except this cousin never hands the beer over. He lets you drink it at his place. Trade records later counted at least $4.8 billion of AI gear with Nvidia inside, all going to her company's Malaysian sister firm, nearly $5 billion to one company most people had never heard of. Real smugglers hid Nvidia chips next to live lobsters. America's big smuggling bust in December 2025 was worth $160 million, about 3% of Mega Speed's haul. Mega Speed didn't need lobsters. It had invoices. >> Cost? >> Some dinners, some whiskey. >> Return? >> $4.8 billion of AI gear our companies can use and a seat next to the man who argues with Washington. >> Did he ever slip you anything under the table? >> Not once. Why pass chips under the table when you can rent the whole warehouse? >> We make friends. >> So what was all of this really for? The seat mattered more than the chips, not for blueprints. Nvidia says customers get zero information relevant to national security. The prize was the man because Washington couldn't make up its mind about what China could buy. >> Your China chip? Blocked. >> So we can't sell it? >> August, you can. We >> take 15%. >> So we can sell it? >> December. And the stronger one, too. We take 25%. >> I'm going to need a bigger whiteboard. >> Blocked. Then 15%. Then 25. >> Washington changes its mind every few months. >> And who does Washington keep hearing from? >> Him. >> That first call alone cost Nvidia 4 and 1/2 billion dollars. In chips, it suddenly couldn't sell. That's about $13 from every person in America gone in one phone call. And through every one of those calls, Jensen made the same argument he'd been making for years, out loud on every stage he could find. Let American chips compete everywhere. >> So you want to sell to China? >> I want the whole world building on American chips. >> Hold that thought. In Taipei in May 2025, he put it bluntly. >> All in all, the export control was a failure. >> A week later to his investors. >> The $50 billion China market is effectively closed to US industry. >> $50 billion. That's about $150 for every American left on the table. That autumn in London, he warned that China was going to win the AI race with cheaper power and fewer rules. That same night, he made sure nobody missed whose side he was on. >> It's vital that America wins by racing ahead in winning developers worldwide. >> That's Jensen in one line. He wants America to win, and he wants to sell the whole world the tools to build on it. Now look at it from Beijing. One chip is worth about $30,000. One conversation between this man and the White House can open a $50 billion market or close it. Which one would you rather have a seat next to? >> What is he telling Washington? >> Let American chips compete everywhere. >> He says that on every stage in the world. Why do we need you? >> Because I hear it first, and I see who he says it to. >> That's the job the memo would later describe. Learn what he knows and sit beside the man Washington listens to. And Washington kept moving. In December 2025, Washington led approved Chinese buyers have the stronger chip. That same week, prosecutors announced that big smuggling bust, the one MegaSpeed made look small. >> You're under arrest for sending these to China. >> Approved. >> What did you just approve? >> Sending these to China. >> Even the approved buyers weren't always what they seemed. >> New Matrix, Beijing. Approved. >> Hello? Anyone? >> The New York Times found that New Matrix, a 17-month-old firm Washington had cleared to handle those chips, had an office that was a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling. On paper, it was approved. On paper, MegaSpeed looked fine, too. Back in the middle of 2025, MegaSpeed had gone quiet. It stopped buying and walked away from an order worth $3.2 billion. In October 2025, Senator Tom Cotton asked Commerce to investigate MegaSpeed. He called the company it came from. >> A Chinese government-owned cloud company. >> The New York Times found the $2 billion of chips. Nvidia said MegaSpeed had no China shareholders. In February 2026, her data center landlord, a business of Bain Capital, gave all the power it had set aside for MegaSpeed to someone else, and the Commerce case moved to the Justice Department. By then, the people listening to her phone had a lot more than boxes. They had watched her for about a year. They photographed the dinners in Singapore. In May 2025, there's even video of the two of them leaving a dinner with AI suppliers in Taipei, Alice a few feet behind him. In the spring of 2026, America wrote it down in a memo overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio. >> Recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Jensen Huang and to shape his lobbying for chip sales to China. >> Who else sees this? >> Just this table. >> The memo went round that small group before President Trump's trip to Beijing in May. According to the New York Times, the president had been briefed and didn't act. Jensen had been left off the list for that plane. Then Trump called him, and Jensen flew to Alaska to climb aboard Air Force One on the way. On the 29th of October 2026, the New York Times broke the story. Alice Huang had been passing information to Beijing, and American intelligence knew it. Nvidia's stock fell about 3%. Jensen told Bloomberg her contacts were about mega speed. >> It was all completely normal and not unusual. >> He said she no longer worked there. Beijing answered too. >> Nothing more than an attempt to smear China. >> Three congressmen asked Jensen in for a closed-door briefing on the 18th of November. Their letter warned of >> significant national security concerns. >> On the 6th of November, the memo itself leaked. >> The spy memo's out. >> I know. >> How bad is it? >> We're up 2.78%. >> Up? >> Today's news will not slow Nvidia. >> But here's the part that still has no answer. Why did nobody tell Jensen? When the government finds a spy close to an American, there's a way to tell them. It's called a defensive briefing. In 2015, the FBI gave one to a congressman in California. >> Your fundraiser works for Chinese intelligence. Then she's gone. >> He cut her off. Jensen Huang never got that visit. The people who knew unmasked his name, photographed his dinners, wrote the memo, and briefed the president. Nobody told the man at the table. He had no idea. And the memo says the friendship became more than a friendship. He was the target, and she got closer than anyone was ever meant to. On the 8th of November, Jensen wrote to his staff. >> I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry. >> Nvidia's board set up a committee of independent directors with outside lawyers. So far, it sees >> no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised. >> Jensen is still CEO, and here's where his story reaches your wallet. Nvidia is now about $8 of every 100 in an S&P 500 index fund. If you have a retirement account, there's a good chance you own a slice of him. >> Wait, I own Nvidia? >> Everybody owns Nvidia. >> And one scary headline from China can move it hard. In January 2025, a Chinese AI lab called Deep Seek shocked Wall Street. >> A Chinese lab built a cheap AI. >> We just lost $589 billion. >> How much is that? >> About $1,700 for every person in America. >> It was the biggest one-day loss in market history. Nvidia reports its earnings on the 17th of November. The congressmen get their briefing the next day, and two weeks later, Jensen walks onto a stage in Washington, the same city as the people who never told him. And Alice Huang, she's gone from Mega Speed. Her name has been taken off its company papers. Nobody has said where she is. Go back to that dinner in Singapore, the candles, the toast to friends. The chair next to Jensen is empty now. >> We make friends. >> America watched her at his table for almost two years and never told him. So who's pulling up a chair next to the people who build America's AI tonight? Jensen ended his letter like this. >> I love our country and our company. I am proud and grateful to be an American.

How Anthropic, the company behind Claude, lost $80 billion in six months, and why it is about to go public in what would be the biggest IPO ever.

Anthropic made about $16 billion in the first half of 2026 and still reported an $80 billion loss. Most of that loss is an accounting charge that grew because the company got more valuable. The bigger number is the $895 billion it has promised to pay for computers over the next few years. Its own CEO has said that a lab that buys too much compute a year too early can go bankrupt.

Would you buy shares in it?

text: In the first 6 months of this year, the company behind Claude lost 80 billion dollars. That's about 18 million dollars an hour, nights included. And Wall Street's answer? We want in. Because Anthropic is about to sell itself to the public in the biggest IPO ever planned. >> Wait, it lost how much? >> 80 billion. >> Okay, where do I tap? >> So, where did the money go? And why has its own CEO already explained on a podcast exactly how a company like his goes bankrupt? San Francisco, January 2021. Seven people leave OpenAI and start a new AI lab. Two of them are siblings. Dario Amodei, the scientist, and his sister Daniela, the one who keeps the company running. Why they left is a whole other story. This one is about the bill. Because building an AI takes hardware, a lot of it. Claude doesn't live in a box under someone's desk. It lives on huge racks of chips in data centers, most of them owned by other companies. Every answer it gives burns time on those chips. The industry calls that compute. Think of it as rent for a brain. And brains are expensive to rent. In May, Anthropic raises its first big round, 124 million dollars. Early on, another investor puts in 500 million. His name is Sam Bankman-Fried. You know how that one ends. In November 2022, his crypto exchange FTX collapses, and his piece of Anthropic gets swept into the bankruptcy with everything else. Then, the people cleaning up the wreck go through the boxes. >> We've got a stake in some AI lab. Is it worth anything? >> It's worth more than he paid. In 2024, the estate sells it for about 1.3 billion dollars. That's roughly 800 million in profit. The most famous crypto fraud of the decade made one great investment, and it was in the AI lab known for being careful. Meanwhile, Claude starts selling. 2023, $41 million. 2024, $386 million. 2025, $4.6 billion. About 10 times bigger every year. The giants want in. Amazon puts in $8 billion. Google signs up for as much as 40, but look at how they pay. They don't buy shares. They hand over cash for a promise, an IOU that turns into shares later. Hold on to that. It comes back with a very big number attached. Because the losses grew even faster. In 2025, Anthropic lost $42 billion. About $9 lost for every dollar sold. That's the kind of math that usually ends a company. Here, investors kept paying more. Even the snacks were losing money. That year, Anthropic let Claude run a small vending machine in its office. The staff nicknamed it Claudius. >> Can you stock tungsten cubes? >> Absolutely. Also, here's a discount code. >> You're selling them for less than you paid. >> Customer loyalty. It also tried to sell $3 Coke Zero to people who could get it for free in the same office. Claudius lost money. Anthropic wrote it up as research. Then, in early 2026, Anthropic got so good at its job that it scared the rest of Wall Street. January 12th, 2026. Anthropic launches Claude Co-work, an AI that doesn't just chat, it does office work. A few weeks later, it adds plugins for 11 different industries. Wall Street does the math. If an AI can do the work, what happens to the companies that sell the tools for that work? In early February, software stocks lose about $285 billion in value. Thomson Reuters, the company behind Reuters, falls 16%. It's worst day ever. >> What did Anthropic release? >> Plugins. >> How many plugins? >> 11. >> That same month, investors put in $30 billion, valuing Anthropic at $380 billion. Google alone puts in 10. And Dario sits down for a long podcast interview and says something about all that rented compute. We'll come back to it. Then the government turns. Anthropic had refused to let Claude be used for mass surveillance at home or for weapons that fire on their own. So, on February 27th, Pete Hegseth's Pentagon labels it a supply chain risk. As of today, Anthropic is a supply chain risk. >> Isn't that label for companies from rival countries? >> Next question. >> He's right, by the way. Anthropic's own lawyers say the losses this year could run from hundreds of millions of dollars to multiple billions. For a company getting ready to ask the public for money, this is how the whole plan dies. It didn't, because the government was never the money. It's less than 2% of Anthropic's sales. The Pentagon deal at the center of the fight was worth about $200 million over 2 years. These days, Anthropic sells that much in about a day. And the spring is the best stretch it has ever had. From April to June, sales hit $11.6 billion. And for the first time, the business makes an operating profit, $974 million. Operating profit means what you make selling the thing minus what it costs to make it. Claude finally paid for itself. In May, investors put in another $65 billion at a value of $965 billion. Remember that first round of $124 million? This one is over 500 times bigger. That's more than double February's price in about 3 months, which is fantastic news. And, as it turns out, the reason it lost $80 billion. June 1st, 2026. Anthropic sends its IPO paperwork to regulators in secret. 11 days later, somebody else goes first. SpaceX lists at $135 a share, worth 1.77 trillion. With almost a third of the shares set aside for regular people. Day one, it closes at 161. Then, it peaks at 211. By the middle of July, it's below where it started. By early August, 108. In about 6 weeks, half the peak is gone. That's the chart Anthropic's bankers get to look at every morning. In October, the books leak. Then, on October 26th, the filing goes public. Its ticker will be ANT. Sales in the first half of the year, $16.3 billion, up from about $1.2 billion a year earlier. Loss, $80.7 billion. The draft's list of things that could go wrong ran 94 pages. >> We're worth more than twice what we were in February. >> Correct. Congratulations. >> Then, why does this say we lost $72 billion? >> Because you're worth more than twice what you were in February. >> Remember the IOUs? Amazon, Google, and other early backers gave Anthropic cash in exchange for shares later. Picture a lemonade stand. Your neighbor gives you $100 today for a slice of the stand handed over down the road. Then, your stand becomes the hottest stand in America. That slice is now worth a fortune, and you still owe it. The accounting rules say, the more your promise is worth, the more you owe. And that jump goes on the books as a loss. Out of the 80.7 billion, 72.4 billion is exactly that, a charge on paper. >> So, did any actual money leave? >> Not for that part. >> Look only at the business of selling Claude, and it lost about $700 million in those 6 months. That's real money. It's also a long way from 80 billion. And over the first 9 months of the year, the business itself brought in $6.6 billion more than it cost to run. Now, flip it around. Amazon owns a pile of those IOUs. On its own books, it reported gains of more than $60 from them. Same promise, one company calls it a loss, the other calls it a profit, and it keeps going. On November 2nd, a new filing. The loss for the first 9 months is $104 billion. That's more than SpaceX raised in its record IPO in June. 94 billion of it is paper, including a $2 billion charge for matching the staff's donations to charity. Meanwhile, Anthropic is sitting on about $132 billion in cash, more than it lost. Both numbers are true. So, the scary number on the thumbnail is mostly a scoreboard of how fast Anthropic's value went up. Case closed? Not quite. Because buried in the same filing is a different number, and that one is real. $895 billion. That's how much Anthropic has signed up to pay for computers in the years ahead. Its sales so far this year? 33 billion. The bill is about 27 times bigger. Here's who gets paid. Broadcom, about 160 billion. Google, 120. Amazon, 110. Microsoft, 45. And about 120 billion to SpaceX's AI business. Yes, that SpaceX. The company whose IPO record Anthropic is chasing is also one of its landlords. Some of it can be canceled or depends on conditions, about 214 billion. But 70 billion is due in the next 12 months, and almost 450 billion before 2031. Why sign for so much, so far ahead? Because compute gets rented years in advance. Book too little and you pay the last-minute price. That's exactly what happened this summer. From July to September, computers cost Anthropic 9.9 billion dollars, up 77%. 5 billion of that was expensive capacity grabbed at short notice. The business slipped back into a small operating loss. >> We need more computers today. >> Today costs more. >> How much have you got? >> About 5 billion dollars worth. >> So, that's one way to get it wrong. Buy too little and you pay through the nose. The other way is to buy too much. Which brings us to you. Here's how a company sells itself to the public. First, the filing. Then, the roadshow. For about a week, bankers pitch the company to the biggest funds on Earth. The funds place orders. This many shares at this price. The night before trading starts, the company and its banks pick the price that fills the book. Then, the market opens and the price does whatever it wants. >> How much did it lose? >> Which loss? >> The big one. >> Oh, that one's good news. >> Then, we'll pay the low end. >> Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley lead it, with 22 banks in all. One more thing to know. Anthropic only gets the money from new shares. When early holders sell their shares in the deal, that money goes to them. And most insiders can't sell for 6 months anyway. The founders, for up to about a year. Regular people get a real seat this time. The filing names six brokers, from Schwab and Fidelity to Robinhood. Reports say the public could get 15 to 20% of the shares. And in September, Anthropic split every share into 10 before the public could buy one. The price talk is 1 and 1/2 to 2 trillion dollars. The big funds are pushing for the low end. Even there, buyers pay about $43 for every dollar of sales Anthropic made over the past 12 months. At 2 trillion, 57. Jay Ritter, the professor Wall Street calls Mr. IPO, has counted. Out of 4,110 American IPOs from 1980 to 2024, only 14 priced at 40 times sales or more. On average, they did 15% worse than the market. Aswath Damodaran, who values companies for a living, called the latest quarter the most telegraphed third quarter number of all time. He puts Anthropic at about 1.475 trillion, just under the low end. Now, back to February and that podcast. Dario was talking about the danger of a lab buying compute too early, years ahead of the customers. He didn't soften it. If I'm just off by a year in that rate of growth, or if the growth rate is 5x a year instead of 10x a year, then you go bankrupt. That's not someone betting against the stock. Why the US stock market crashed on Thursday, 5 November 2026, and whether it was the AI bubble popping.

On Thursday the S&P 500 fell more than 4%, the Dow lost 1,833 points and Nvidia dropped 9%, losing more than $400 billion in a single morning. The sell-off followed a midterm election in which voters turned against AI data centres, a report that 600,000 Nvidia chips were stuck in Hong Kong, and big funds selling the year's winners to lock in their gains. It came after a month in which AI stocks had already lost about $5 trillion.

text: On Thursday, Nvidia lost more than $400 billion in a single morning, and it hadn't done anything wrong. Nobody had. No bank failed, no law passed. The economy looked fine. The S&P 500 still lost more than $2 trillion by mid-morning, and the Nasdaq needed just 6 minutes to give back a rally that was 1 day old. So why did the stock market just crash? And was this the AI bubble popping? >> Best day after a midterm since 1982. Does this come with a receipt? >> The short answer is an election. 600,000 chips stuck in Hong Kong and some very rich people locking in a very good year. The long answer starts a month earlier, on the 6th of October in Santa Clara, California. That day, Nvidia closed at the highest price it had ever had. A month before, it was worth about $5.4 trillion, roughly 8 cents of every dollar in the whole S&P 500. If you own a plain index fund, the safe, boring kind everyone recommends, you own a lot of Nvidia. Add the rest of the Magnificent Seven, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and Tesla, and about $35 of every 100 in that fund sits on seven companies. >> I'm diversified. 500 companies. >> Seven of them are a third of the pie. >> That is a big slice. >> Even at the dot com peak, the market wasn't this lopsided, and most of those giants are betting on the same thing. That bet is expensive. This year, the four biggest cloud companies plan to spend over $700 billion building data centers. Next year, more than a trillion. The biggest line on that shopping list says Nvidia, whose last quarter brought in $96 billion, more than double the year before. By late October, investors were staring at four cracks. Crack one, the money goes in a circle. Nvidia invests in its own customers, the AI labs and chip rental firms that then buy Nvidia chips. It owns a stake in Coreweave, which rents those chips out and agreed to buy up to $6.3 billion of the computing power Coreweave can't sell. Nvidia's own finance chief knows how that sounds. We know some will call this circular financing. >> Here here's a few billion dollars. >> Wow. What should I spend it on? >> Funny you should ask. >> Crack two, the chips are the collateral. Firms like Coreweave borrowed huge sums to buy chips, rented them out, and pledged those same chips to borrow more. At one point, Coreweave owed over $5 for every dollar of equity. Fine, while a used chip holds its value, but Nvidia brings out a new generation every year or two, and each one makes the last one worth less. And Michael Burry, who called the housing crash, says the giants book their servers as lasting longer than they do, which flatters profits. The nightmare, one borrower misses one payment, the lender grabs the chips to sell, and everyone learns that afternoon what a used AI chip is worth in a hurry. It hasn't happened, but every chip investor has thought about it. Crack three, who's paying? By the end of July, Nvidia was owed about $63 billion for chips it had shipped but not been paid for yet. And this year, just three buyers made up more than two-fifths of its sales. Picture a restaurant where three tables order two of every five plates, and a lot of the food goes on a tab. Crack four, the plug. You can buy a chip. You can't buy electricity that doesn't exist. In Northern Virginia, the data center capital of the world, the wait to hook a new building up to the grid had stretched to about seven years, and the power that does exist, somebody pays for. On America's biggest grid across 13 states, power plants get paid just to stand ready, and families cover that in their bills. Then the data centers piled in. Households there were paying an estimated $25 to $30 a month more than in 2024, and the grid's own watchdog blamed data centers first. >> Why is the electric bill up again? >> Hi neighbor. Nobody reads a spending report. Everybody reads their power bill. Hold that thought. Wall Street had its own bad news. On October 29th, Google had its worst trading day ever. The next day, Intel fell by a quarter. Chip stocks slid into a bear market, and Apple, the boring one, passed Nvidia in value. By the 2nd of November, the 47 biggest AI and chip stocks had lost about $5 trillion since the top. That's about what the whole .com crash wiped out, and that took two and a half years. This took four weeks. Then came the election. Tuesday, the 3rd of November, Democrats won the House. Then they won the Senate. Further down the ballot in 10 states, there were 41 local votes on data centers. Voters went against them in 40. 21 of those were in Ohio. The one town that said yes was Harwood, North Dakota. >> Ohio, no. Ohio, no. Ohio, no. Ohio. >> Hi, yes, over here. >> That's the power bill showing up at the ballot box. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown beat John Husted, who'd been called the face of data centers. In Texas, Elon Musk, the cycle's biggest donor with at least $474 million, lost both big races. His reaction? >> Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now. >> Here's why a town vote moves Wall Street. A data center needs land, power, and a permit, and all three are local. Goldman Sachs figured moratoriums like these could hit about 45% of America's planned data center expansion. And the bigger fear was Washington. For years, AI was mostly left alone to build. Now, a Democratic Congress, elected the same night voters said no to data centers, might want rules on where data centers go, who pays for their power, and how fast the build out runs. One congressman, Robert Garcia, had two words for AI executives, lawyer up. >> So, data centers. So, data centers. >> We were just leaving. >> No rule has passed, not one. It was the fear of a rule that did the selling. That trillion dollar shopping list had picked up some small print, if they let us build it. And on Wednesday, Wall Street partied anyway. The Dow jumped 1,569 points, about 3%. It's best day after a midterm since 1982, and oil fell more than 9%. Traders loved the cheap oil. They hadn't gotten to the new Congress yet. The party lasted one day. That morning, Vice President JD Vance had posted on X. >> The reason we lost is the war. >> The war with Iran. That raised hopes of a deal, and oil fell. By Thursday morning, traders doubted it, and oil climbed again. Then, before the opening bell, Reuters dropped the next problem. About 600,000 of Nvidia's H200 chips were sitting in Hong Kong, waiting for Beijing to let them in. Washington had cleared the sales last winter, case by case, with a 25% tariff. In August, Beijing let companies use them in Hong Kong. Into mainland China, in bulk, still waiting. >> You said we can sell them. >> You can. 25% please. >> They're in Hong Kong. Can they come in? >> They're not moving. Not yet. >> The strange part, Nvidia had already taken a $400 million hit on H200s that nobody bought, and the ones that did buyers couldn't get through the door. 9:30, the bell rings in New York. It takes the Nasdaq six minutes to give back the whole rally. So much for Wednesday. 10:35, the Nasdaq is down 4% and the Dow 700 points. Across the S&P 500, more than $2 trillion has vanished, and more than $400 billion of it is Nvidia alone. That's about twice Amazon's entire building budget for the year. 11:17, the VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, is up 65%. Think of it as the price of crash insurance, and everybody wants some. 11:37, the Dow is on track for its worst second day after a midterm in records going back to 1896. 1:38, AMD's boss, Lisa Su, speaks up with her stock down 15%. >> I think the market can sometimes be a little bit shortsighted. >> 2:58, and this is where ordinary people come in. Maybe you're at work, checking your phone under the desk. You own a plain S&P 500 fund. If it holds a quarter of a million dollars, Nvidia alone took about $990 out of it that morning. By now, small investors have sold on net $358 million of stock, the most since March 2020. >> Buy the dip? >> Or sell the dip? Or sell the dip? >> Viraj Patel at Vanda Research called it a total capitulation by retail investors with no signs of buying the dip. 3:06, Charlie McElligott, a strategist at Nomura, explains who's really selling. >> They're shooting the generals. >> The generals are the year's biggest winners. Hedge funds had made a fortune in 2026, and with two months to go, they sold the winners to lock it in. Computer-driven funds and funds on borrowed money were forced to sell too, and nobody stepped in to buy. >> Great year. >> Let's bank it. Sell the winners. >> Which ones? >> Yes. Yes. >> Single name stock moves are absolutely bonkers. >> >> 4:00 the closing bell. The Dow lost 1,833 points. The S&P fell over 4%. The Nasdaq fell 5 and 1/2. It's biggest drop in 19 months and is now in a correction, at least 10% below its high. Chip stocks had their worst day since March 2020. Nvidia closed at $181, down more than 9%. And while everything burned, AppLovin rose almost 30%. And Goldman Sachs picked that day to name 109 new partners. It's biggest class since 2010. >> Honestly, honestly, honestly, great day to get promoted. >> It's easy to think a crash like this only hurts rich people. It doesn't. Around 70 million Americans save in a 401k, mostly through the same index funds. And the pensions of teachers and firefighters hold them too. When the seven giants fall, they fall too. It goes deeper than stocks. Data centers run on borrowed money, much of it raised from insurers and pension funds. Pimco bought a big piece of the bonds for Meta's giant Louisiana data center with savers money. And Washington has moved to open 401ks to this kind of lending. So your retirement may be quietly lending to a half built building. And some get hit without owning a share. The electricians, some making $260,000 a year on data center jobs. And the diners that feed them. Thursday didn't stop that work. But if the spending stops, it lands there first. If you're 25, Thursday was a sale. If you're 62 and retiring in the spring, it was a very long day. So who do you get angry at? Every crash wants a villain. 2008 had the banks. Thursday doesn't really have one. >> I just didn't want >> the bill. >> I just wanted to keep my good year. >> I just said not yet. >> I just sold chips. >> Every one of those choices made sense on its own. They just all landed on the same morning. So here's why the stock market crashed. A market that's 1/3 AI had been sliding for a month. Then in three days, voters elected a Congress that might rain in data centers. Beijing left 600,000 chips at the door and funds sitting on a great year cashed out. Nothing broke. The fear did it. It isn't new either. In the 1840s, Britain went mad for railways and at the peak it was pouring about 7% of its economy into track. Railway shares lost nearly 2/3 of their value and a third or more of the approved lines never got built. But many of the lines that did get built are still part of Britain's railway today. Here's the catch. A railway can wait for its trains. A chip sitting in a dark building just gets older. So was Thursday the AI bubble popping? Not yet. Both tariff crash days in April 2025 were bigger and together erased a record $6.6 trillion. Jobless claims were near their lowest since 1969 and no rule had passed. Bernie Sanders called for a national moratorium on data centers. >> Americans don't want big tech oligarchs wrecking the environment. >> A call, not a bill. A bubble doesn't pop when prices fall. It pops when the money stops. On Thursday, the money hadn't stopped. Nvidia's sales were still doubling. The giants were still expected to spend more than a trillion dollars next year. But here's the part almost nobody noticed. A week before the crash, one giant blinked. Microsoft cut its spending plan from $175 billion to 170. That's less than 3%. Tiny, but it's a foot moving toward the break. And on Tuesday, the people who pay the electric bill elected a Congress that might want to say in where the buildings go. So Thursday wasn't the pop. It was the day the market noticed there's a pin and that voters, Washington and Beijing all have a hand on it. Nvidia is now about a quarter below its October record. Its next report is due on the 17th of November and the 600,000 chips are still in Hong Kong. The rally died in 6 minutes. What happens next gets decided much more slowly by permits, power lines, and an electric bill on a kitchen table in Ohio. On Thursday, Lisa Su said the market can be a little bit short-sighted. That afternoon, it might have been the furthest it had looked in months.
